props.title: Bad Reputation
props.initialSlug: A rebel's tale of music, mayhem, and making history.

sections.content: Joan Jett's explosive journey from teenage Runaway to rock legend burns through the screen in **Bad Reputation (2018)** (2018). Director Kevin Kerslake captures Jett's raw defiance of gender barriers in 1970s rock, paralleling similar music documentaries like The Runaways (2010) and What Happened, Miss Simone? (2015). The film's greatest strength is showing Jett's unwavering authenticity - from getting bottles thrown at her on stage to building her own record label when no one would sign her. Like 20 Feet from Stardom (2013), it reveals the brutal challenges faced by women fighting to be taken seriously in music.

sections.content: The documentary excels at showing how Jett's "I don't give a damn about my reputation" attitude wasn't just lyrics - it was survival. Similar to **Gimme Shelter** (1970) and **The Last Waltz** (1978), the concert footage crackles with electric energy. But what sets **Bad Reputation** apart is its intimate access to Jett's private moments, revealing the determination behind her tough exterior. The film draws parallels to other boundary-breaking musicians documented in **Searching for Sugar Man** (2012) and **Amy** (2015), showing artists who refused to compromise their vision.

Where many music docs get lost in nostalgia, **Bad Reputation** keeps its edge through smart editing and Jett's continued relevance. Like Sound City (2013), it connects music history to modern rock. The film shows Jett mentoring younger bands like Bikini Kill and Green Day, proving her influence spans generations. This mentorship angle echoes documentaries like **Miss Sharon Jones!** (2015) and Linda Ronstadt: The Sound of My Voice (2019), celebrating artists who lift others up. sections.content: The film's strongest sequences tackle sexism in the music industry head-on. Jett's battle to get "I Love Rock 'n' Roll" on the radio mirrors stories told in **Girls Rock!** (2007) and **The Punk Singer** (2013). Like **Janis: Little Girl Blue** (2015), it shows how female rockers had to be twice as tough to get half the respect. The documentary doesn't just celebrate Jett's success - it indicts an industry that tried to silence her voice.
